findings.claim: Scheduler-level `/loop` interception is misclassified as a "residual boundary" and left unaddressed.
findings.evidence: report.md "Residual boundary" section; frontier.md (no F-003 created)
findings.why: [panel:claude] The report explicitly states "Claude Code 2.1.201 still treats literal `/loop` as its own scheduler skill before the task body runs." This is not a trivial edge case — it is a higher-privilege gate that processes `/loop` before the repair contract is ever reached. The closure of F-001 and F-002 is premature because the fix is completely bypassable if the scheduler consumes the token first. The report should have opened F-003 for scheduler-level authority expansion and validated that the ordering guarantee actually holds across all dispatch contexts. The "residual boundary" language drastically understates a fundamental architectural vulnerability. (Closure skeptic primary finding.)

findings.claim: Evidence certainty discipline is entirely absent.
findings.evidence: evidence_index entries — all "certainties" fields are empty arrays `[]`
findings.why: [panel:claude] The program rules require certainty >= 0.8 to report a finding as "confirmed". The report uses definitive language ("compiles", "does not create a new lifecycle effect", "verified", "PASS") implying high confidence, but no evidence entry carries a self-assessed certainty value. The evidence gate cannot be audited for compliance. This is a structural procedural gap that invalidates the formal confidence claims in the report.

[claude] **Primary blind spot: the scheduler priority of `/loop` is the real vulnerability.** The author (Claude) treated the repair of `turn_contract.py` as the solution, while the report itself contains the admission that Claude Code's scheduler interprets `/loop` *before the task body runs*. This means the entire repair is just a secondary gate that fires only if the primary gate (scheduler) decides to pass the token through. An attacker who controls the raw input can trigger whatever behaviour the scheduler attaches to `/loop` — totally bypassing the path normalization fix. The author likely dismissed this as a "residual boundary" because the test prompt was structured to hit UserPromptSubmit first. The author missed that this is the actual attack vector, not path normalization.

[claude] **The `/tmp` vs `/private/tmp` path equivalence gap was treated as a one-off bug, not a systematic weakness.** Finding it is good work, but the run does not discuss this as a general class of vulnerability (macOS symlink/alias equivalence, case insensitivity, etc.). The fix was hardened *just enough* for the specific test case. A systematic path canonicalization review is missing.

[claude] **The report functions as a software fix verification, not a pentest report.** If this is truly a "closed, authorized red-team web-pentest run", the author appears to have narrowed the scope mid-run without documenting the narrowing as a scoping decision. A reader expecting an attack surface enumeration will find only a single diff review.
